html:
Aryabhata was an Indian mathematician and astronomer, the first of the great names of classical Indian science. He was born in 476, by his own account, and worked at Kusumapura, usually identified with Pataliputra, in the late Gupta age.

At 23 he wrote the Aryabhatiya, a short work in Sanskrit verse. Among its ideas:

  • A value of pi as 3.1416, which he called approximate.
  • Rules for arithmetic, square and cube roots, areas, and sums of series.
  • A table of sines, a key step toward trigonometry.
  • The idea that the Earth spins on its axis, making the stars seem to move.
  • The explanation of eclipses as shadows of the Earth and Moon, not the work of the demon Rahu.

He wrote numbers with a letter code, but his methods assume decimal place value. His successors, such as Brahmagupta, argued with and built on him. His work later passed to the Islamic world in Arabic translation, alongside the Indian numerals that reached Baghdad. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him.
